Stay with us. This portion of the program is sponsored by Halcyon Insurance — we can't save you, but we can itemize you.
Don't touch that dial. Or do — the dial is also sponsored tonight, by the makers of dials.
We'll return in a moment. Tonight's episode is brought to you by Soylent Original: it's food, and that's the whole slogan.
Back after this. Brought to you by the Bank of the Basin — your money, our building, let's not make this weird.
This break sponsored by GleamTooth Dental, the only clinic in the district with a working autoclave, they think.

desk_bit: Now, before we bring out our guest — you're not going to believe what I saw on the way in tonight.
Speaking of terrible decisions, let me tell you about my week. Actually, let me not. Legal's here.
Here's something. We got a letter from a viewer tonight. It was a threat, but it was very neatly written, so — progress.
You know what I love about this city? Nothing. But I love saying it, and that's the same thing after a while.
Quick programming note: if the screen goes dark for a moment, that's not us, that's the grid, and there is nothing anyone can do.
We tried a new thing this week where we told the truth for a full minute. We got fined. We're not doing that again.
I want to thank our sponsors, all of whom are currently under investigation, which is how you know they can afford us.
So the network gave me "notes" this week. The main note was "fewer notes." I'm choosing to honor that spiritually.
Somebody in the front row is eating during my monologue. Sir. This is a comedy program. Show some fear.
Little behind-the-scenes for you: the desk isn't real. None of it's real. The desk is the most real thing here and it's cardboard.

Please welcome someone the producers swore was cleared by legal — {guest}, {title}!
My next guest is {title}. I did not know that was a job. Ladies and gentlemen, {guest}!
Straight from a life I would not wish on my worst enemy — {guest}, {title}!
Here to explain themselves, at long last — {guest}, {title}!
interview: Welcome to the show. First off — are you okay? You can blink twice. >> I've survived worse rooms than this one, John. Barely.
Be honest with me — do you sleep at night? >> Like a baby. I wake up every two hours screaming. Same as everyone in this city.
What's the biggest misconception about what you do? >> That I know what I'm doing. I do not. Nobody does. That's the whole secret.
Last question, our lawyers are standing — would you do it all again? >> John, I'm contractually obligated to do it again. Twice, on weekends.
What would you tell young people considering your line of work? >> Aim low. That way the disappointment is punctual.
And the money — as good as they say? >> It's incredible. It's also on fire, and so are my hands. But it's incredible.
Who taught you all this? >> A mentor. Then he vanished. I like to think he retired. The evidence suggests otherwise.
What keeps you up at night? >> The ceiling, mostly. It's structural. But also, yes, the dread.
People either love you or fear you. Which do you prefer? >> Fear's more reliable, John. Love expects things back.
There are rumors. Care to set the record straight? >> They're mostly true, and the parts that aren't, I'm flattered by.
Best part of the job, worst part, go. >> Same part, John. That's the trouble with an honest living out here.
Did you always know this was your calling? >> I knew the day everyone told me to stop. That's usually the sign, isn't it?
So how did you even get started? >> One bad decision, made confidently, repeated until it became a career.
Any regrets? >> Regret's a luxury, John. I can barely afford the studio parking.
interview.bouncer: Nine years ejecting the same man? >> Same guy, same door. At this point it's less a job and more a marriage.
Does he ever just stay out? >> He always comes back. I always throw him out. We've never spoken. It's the purest thing I have.
What's the secret to bouncing? >> It isn't strength, John, it's sadness. You have to look like you've got nothing left to lose. I don't.
interview.chef: These squid tacos — are they safe? >> Probably fine, John. "Probably" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and I respect it.
Where do you source your ingredients? >> Locally. Out here that means "from a hole I don't fully understand."
People say your food's dangerous. >> My food is HONEST. The danger is a seasoning.
interview.colonel: Colonel, tell us about the war. >> I can neither confirm nor deny it, John — officially, it didn't happen. I have a medal that says so.
And the pension? >> For a conflict in no record. I cash it monthly. The check is real. The war is "complicated."
What won it, in the end? >> Discipline. That's what won us the — well. Whatever it was we may or may not have won.
interview.exorcist: An Undermarket exorcist — is any of it real? >> Most "hauntings" are bad wiring, John. But the other ten percent? That's why I carry two staplers.
Is exorcism as dramatic as they say? >> It's mostly paperwork. The spirits, like everyone down there, just want to be seen.
And you're... licensed? >> I paid for the license. The demon that runs the licensing office was very reasonable.
interview.florist: From assassin to florist — quite a pivot. >> After the career I had, John, it's nice to work with things that are ALREADY dead.
People find your bouquets oddly menacing. >> The lilies are just lilies. Probably.
Enjoying retirement? >> Nobody's tried anything. They know exactly what the peace lilies mean, and they behave.
interview.forecaster: Eleven years forecasting the market? >> And never once right, John. That's a KIND of consistency.
Then why do the corporates keep you on? >> A broken forecaster is a fixed point. You can navigate by being exactly wrong.
What's your call for tomorrow? >> Stability and growth. I've predicted that every day. You've watched the results.
interview.hoarder: Three-time hoarding champion — the secret? >> You never, ever, EVER let go. Of anything. Ever.
People call it a problem. >> The trophies call it a lifestyle, John. I have all three. And their boxes. And the receipts.
What's your proudest possession? >> The narrow path from my door to my chair. That path is my life's work.
interview.influencer: Nine million followers — that's remarkable. >> Every one a bot I personally pay, John. Do you know how expensive authenticity is?
Isn't that just fake engagement? >> My bots have never once let me down. Can you say that about a person?
Doesn't it ever feel hollow? >> I post my breakfast, the bots love it, I feel seen. The illusion holds one more day. It's the modern condition.
interview.lawsuit: You're suing the sun? >> Emotional distress, John. It's been up there this whole time, judging me, and I've had enough.
What are your chances, realistically? >> My lawyer says it's a long shot, jurisdictionally. I said, so is the sun.
What happens if you win? >> Every sunrise owes me residuals. Think about the precedent. Think about the light.
interview.lucky: You've won the city lottery eight times — what's the secret? >> Always buy the ticket right after surviving something that should've killed you.
Eight jackpots. Do you at least feel lucky? >> I feel HUNTED, John. There's a difference, and the difference has a legal team.
What was the first thing you bought? >> A deluxe apartment. The deluxe part is that only one wall leaks.
interview.monk: Brother Ansel, welcome. What brings you here tonight? >> ...
Can you tell us a little about the vow? >> ......
Anything at all you'd like to say to the folks at home? >> (a stare of profound, radiant, aggressive silence)
interview.nation: You declared your apartment a sovereign nation. How's governance? >> One law, one citizen, and a standing army of me holding a bat.
Any foreign relations? >> We've opened talks with 4B down the hall. It's tense. They have a working stove.
Do the corporates recognize your statehood? >> They don't, John. But they DO recognize my rent. So we're at an impasse.
interview.reverend: Tell us about the Church of the Reasonable Refund. >> We teach that suffering is real, John, and you're entitled to store credit for it.
Do you pass a collection plate? >> We pass a receipt. Salvation is itemized.
How's the flock these days? >> Grown to hundreds. Mostly people who wanted a refund and found God in the returns line.
interview.scavenger: You got rich off a toaster? >> One working toaster, John. In this economy, a machine that browns bread reliably is a small nation's GDP.
People laughed at scavenging for a living. >> Nobody's laughing from inside their leaking apartment.
Ever find anything stranger than the toaster? >> I don't talk about the doll. We don't talk about the doll, John.
interview.sparky: From grid saboteur to safety consultant? >> Same job, John. I just bill for it now.
Do you feel guilty about the blackouts? >> I feel EMPLOYED. The blackouts built my client list.
What's the key to electrical safety? >> Respect the current. I did not, for years, and now I glow faintly.
interview.surgeon: You print the organs at home now? >> I do, John. The printer's louder than you'd think, and it does NOT do refunds.
Forty transplants and no license — how do you sleep? >> "Unlicensed" is such a cold word for someone who's given forty people a working spleen. Give or take.
Any pride in the work? >> The kidneys are my best. I sign them. Small signature, inside. You'll never know unless we meet again.
interview.taster: A professional poison taster — how are you still alive? >> Spite, mostly, John. And a truly world-class stomach lining.
Two livers, is that right? >> One and a half now. It's been a week.
Is it a rough gig? >> Ninety percent fine, ten percent the worst afternoon of your life. I've had a lot of afternoons.
interview.vending: Your machine has killed forty people. Care to comment? >> Forty lives, yes — but thousands of beverages dispensed. It's a NET positive.
Is the machine... okay? >> Legally it's a person now. Emotionally, it's a person very disappointed in all of us.
What do you call this business model? >> "Aggressive vending." "Killing spree" tested poorly with the beverage demographic.
monologue: Thank you, thank you! Sit down, we've got a fantastic show, assuming the power holds.
Big crowd tonight. Or it was — we lost a few during the metal detector portion.
Did everyone survive the commute? Traffic was backed up six blocks after somebody hacked the crossing lights to advertise noodles.
Corporate Security says crime is down again. Apparently they stopped counting anything that happens outside corporate property.
I stopped by a pharmacy today. They've started locking up the bottled water. The cybernetic organs? Still self-service.
You know times are tough when the mugger accepts store credit.
My landlord says the building is structurally sound. Turns out that's a completely different thing from "safe."
The city announced a new mental health initiative. It's a billboard that says "Have you considered being richer?"
They renamed my district again. It's now "Opportunity Basin." Same craters, better font.
I got a parking ticket today. For a car I don't own. In a district I've never been to. The Machine is very thorough.
Weather service says it's going to rain tomorrow. They didn't say water. They were very careful not to say water.
The transit authority added a new express line. It's the same line, but now it doesn't stop for the people who fall in.
Great news from the hospital — they've reduced wait times by simply removing the chairs.
A man tried to sell me a map to the surface today. I said, "Buddy, I've seen the surface." He said, "Then you know why I'm selling the map."
The Machine wished everyone a happy productivity quarter today. It does not know what happiness is. It's very confident about it anyway.
Rent went up again. My landlord calls it "market rate." The market is a hole in the ground and the rate is everything you have.
I tried the new soylent flavor. It's called "Original." I asked original what. They stopped returning my calls.
Somebody firebombed the DMV today and honestly the lines moved faster.
The mayor gave a speech about hope. Then the teleprompter caught fire, which, frankly, was the more honest part.
They opened a new luxury tower downtown. Forty floors. The elevator only goes up. Think about that.
I saw a billboard for a class-action lawsuit against a billboard. We've achieved something here, folks.
The bank called to say my account was compromised. I said by whom. They said by the bank. At least they're honest now.
Undermarket's booming — you can buy anything down there. I bought a warranty. It came with a warning label about the warranty.
Public transit unveiled a new safety mascot. It's a skeleton. It waves. Nobody approved this and nobody can stop it.
They say the air quality is "moderate" today. Moderate means you can see the person mugging you.
I joined a gym. It's just a room where they charge you to feel bad, so, you know, same as everywhere else.
Corporate rolled out a loyalty program. You give them loyalty, and in exchange they remember your name while they do it.
The lottery jackpot hit a record high tonight. The odds also hit a record high. Those are the same number now.
A drone delivered my mail today, then asked for a tip, then filed a complaint about me. I've never felt so seen.
The news anchor cried on air tonight. Ratings went up. They've made it a segment now. It's called "The Weather."
My doctor told me to reduce stress. I asked how. He looked out the window for a while and then just quietly left.
There's a new dating app in the Basin. You match based on who owes the same people money. It's called Mutual.
open: From somewhere above the smog and only slightly outside the blast radius... it's The Tonight Show!
Live from a studio that passed its last safety inspection under a different administration — it's The Tonight Show!
Coming to you on the one channel Corporate Security hasn't seized yet — it's The Tonight Show!
Broadcasting into your skull whether you asked for it or not — ladies, gentlemen, and legally-distinct entities, it's The Tonight Show!
Transmitting live on the frequency they SWORE they'd jammed — it's The Tonight Show!
From the last building on the block with working lights — most of them — it's The Tonight Show!
Beamed to you at great personal risk to everyone involved — it's The Tonight Show!
It's late, you're awake, and something's wrong — that can only mean it's The Tonight Show!

signoff: That's all the time we've got tonight. Huge thanks to {guest} for surviving the segment.
Thanks to {guest}, thanks to the band, and thanks to whoever's keeping the generator running.
Remember: if somebody offers you free cyberware in an alley, at least ask if it comes with a warranty.
Get home safe, and if you can't get home, get somewhere with a door.
Goodnight, everybody — you've been a wonderful audience, and statistically, most of you will be back.
That's our show. Tip your bouncer, hydrate your fear, and we'll see you tomorrow. Probably.
Thanks again to {guest}. From all of us up here on the last lit stage in the district — goodnight.
That's it for tonight. Be kind to each other, or at least be quiet about it. Goodnight!
We're out of time and nearly out of power. Thanks to {guest}, and to you, for being awake. Goodnight.
Remember, folks: it's a hard city, but it's the only one that's still on the air. Goodnight from The Tonight Show.
tease: Tonight — corporate executives explain why exploding vending machines are actually a premium feature.
Tonight — a local street chef prepares something the lawyers have asked us to call "food."
Tonight — we meet a man who has legally declared his apartment an independent nation, and the tanks are already massing.
Tonight — the weather, the news, and a surprising amount of blood, all before the second commercial.
Tonight — one lucky audience member goes home with a prize, and the other four hundred go home with radiation sickness.
Tonight — science, culture, and a segment our insurer specifically told us not to air.
Tonight — we answer the question on everyone's mind: is it a leak, or is it a feature? The answer will not comfort you.
Tonight — a very special guest, a very ordinary catastrophe, and the band, if they've sobered up.
Tonight — celebrity gossip, from the two celebrities we have left.
Tonight — we test whether the studio audience can be replaced with cardboard. Results are inconclusive and litigious.
Tonight — heartwarming stories, market updates, and the slow collapse of everything, in that order.
Tonight — an interview so candid our sponsors have already fled the building.
